concept: deixis
statement: Deictic expressions are interpreted relative to utterance-act roles, time or place, normally from the speaker/writer's perspective but sometimes from a shifted centre such as the reader of a public notice or a person whose thoughts are reported.
condition: Identify utterance-anchored person, temporal and locative reference (I, you, now, yesterday, here, this, that), while permitting contextually shifted reader-centred and reported-perspective interpretations rather than requiring every example to use the speaker's immediate time and place.

exceptions.description: The deictic centre may shift to the current reader of a notice or to a reported person's perspective rather than the speaker/writer's own time.

Look at that.

I will return next week. [I and next week anchored to the speaker]

concept: anaphora and pro-forms
statement: Anaphora is the relation between an anaphor and its antecedent: the anaphor's interpretation derives from the antecedent; anaphors may be personal pronouns and other pro-forms (so, do so, one) or gaps, and the relation can be shown by co-indexing.

concept: Backshifted perspective outside subordinate clauses
statement: A main-clause interrogative in a narrative may use non-deictic backshift to represent a character's thoughts, including free indirect thought without an overt reporting verb.
condition: A narrative or parenthetical thought report adopts a character's earlier time of orientation rather than the narrator's current speech time.

correct.text: Would the train still be there when she reached the platform, Mara wondered.
The visitor was worried. Had he missed the final bus? Would anyone help him?

concept: Backshifted and non-backshifted reported present
statement: A past-time report can use either a backshifted preterite anchored to the original utterance or a present anchored to the reporting utterance.
condition: The reported proposition concerns a state that may still hold at the time of the later report.

correct.text: Nina said that the office was busy.
Nina said that the office is busy.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Burton-Roberts crosswalk not independently checked.

concept: Reported-content orientation rather than tense rewrite
statement: Backshift describes non-deictic tense interpretation of reported content, not a grammatical transformation from an underlying quotation.
condition: The reported proposition is expressed through an embedded clause without reproducing the original speaker's exact words.

correct.text: The guide mentioned that the northern path was closed.
Mila believed that the southern gate was unlocked.

concept: Four tense patterns in indirect reported content
statement: Reported present, simple preterite, present perfect and past perfect have different backshift alternatives; only the first three permit an additional distinct backshifted form.
condition: A past reporting predicate embeds content with one of the four major tense forms of the original utterance.

correct.text: Lina said that the gate was open. [present-to-preterite]
Lina said that the inspector had inspected the gate. [past-to-past-perfect]
Lina said that the inspector had already left. [perfect report]

concept: No separate triple-past morphological backshift
statement: An original past-perfect report cannot be backshifted to a new three-layer past tense because English has no corresponding ordinary triple-past tense form.
condition: A report already represents an event through preterite perfect and is embedded in an additional past reporting clause.

correct.text: The witness said that the vehicle had left earlier.
The editor said that the publisher had already sent the proofs.

concept: Backshift choices form a prefix through embedded clauses
statement: In a complex indirect report of an original present-tense clause, valid combinations backshift all the relevant finite levels, just the first level, or none; an unshifted higher complement cannot be followed by a further backshift solely for that same reporting relation.
condition: A nested indirect report has a past reporting verb, a finite embedded matrix clause and a further subordinate present-time relation inherited from the original utterance.
violation: A nested, non-backshifted reported present event is paired with a further backshifted preterite for the same original temporal relation, despite the higher event already having deictic tense.

exceptions.description: The restriction concerns backshifted subordinate time in the same original reported utterance, not an independently interpreted earlier event or another kind of subordinate relation.

correct.text: Ari said that she was packing before the guests returned.
Ari said that she was packing before the guests return.
Ari said that she is packing before the guests return.

incorrect.text: Ari said that she is packing before the guests returned.
Nora said that she is travelling before the meeting began.

concept: Non-backshifted tense must preserve temporal relation
statement: A present-tense non-backshifted report is pragmatically licensed when the situation's relation to the reporting time can reasonably match its relation to the original speaker's time.
condition: An indirect report keeps deictic present rather than using a past tense oriented to the prior utterance.

correct.text: Jon said the laboratory is open. [if it remains open]
Jon said the concert starts tomorrow. [if the start is still future]

concept: Persistence of a reported state affects tense choice
statement: Present-tense indirect reporting is more likely when a state commonly lasts across the interval between original and reported utterances.
condition: A reporting speaker chooses whether to use present tense for an enduring condition or a short-lived one.

correct.text: She said the library is in the old town. [long-lived location]
She said she had a cold. [short-term past condition]

concept: Future reference in non-backshifted indirect report
statement: A present-tense future-oriented content clause is appropriate only if the projected event remains in the future relative to the act of reporting.
condition: An original future-present event is retold after some time has elapsed.

correct.text: On Monday Rosa said that the exhibition opens next Friday. [reported before Friday]
After the event, Rosa said the exhibition opened the previous Friday. [retrospective report]

concept: Reporter endorsement favours but does not force present tense
statement: A reporter who endorses the content often chooses non-backshifted present, while doubt or rejection often favours backshift; neither tendency is obligatory.
condition: The truth of the earlier proposition is adopted or questioned by the later reporter.

correct.text: He told us the gate is accessible, so we can go through it.
He told us the gate was accessible, but it is firmly locked.

concept: Original belief focus favours backshift
statement: Backshift is favoured when the reporting clause highlights what somebody believed at the earlier time rather than what is now known.
condition: A report focuses the contrast between an earlier belief and current evidence.

correct.text: I thought the blue folder was mine, but it belongs to her.
I believed the figures were correct; now the auditor disagrees.

concept: Present tense reports an event still projected after now

condition: The reporter relates an earlier announced plan to the time of the new report.

correct.text: Mara said she is leaving this weekend. [weekend still upcoming]
Mara said she was leaving that weekend. [the report need not assert a currently upcoming departure]

concept: Present perfect matrix often favours deictic report
statement: A present-perfect reporting clause tends to favour an unshifted present content tense, while simple preterite reporting more often favours past backshift.
condition: The matrix predicate reports speech through has said or said and embeds a proposition interpreted at reporting time.

concept: Simplification of a reported original past event
statement: When an earlier utterance contained simple preterite, an indirect report may preserve that preterite rather than shift it to past perfect if the earlier-time meaning is already clear.
condition: The complement reports a finished event whose past relation is evident independently of a second past layer.

correct.text: They asked where I was born.
They asked where I had been born.

concept: Temporal ambiguity can require past perfect in report
statement: When a simple preterite complement would naturally be read as backshifted present, past perfect may be needed to report that an original state was already in the past.
condition: The reporter must distinguish an original present state from an original past state under a past reporting verb.

concept: Current state backshift differs from original past-time report
statement: A reported preterite describing a state is often read as a backshift of present; a past perfect can mark that the state itself preceded the earlier report.
condition: A past reporting clause embeds a stative verb without an independent past-time adjunct.

correct.text: The visitor said he liked the apartment. [compatible with then-present liking]

concept: Primary preterite more often directly deictic than perfect
statement: Primary preterite typically anchors reference time to the speech time, whereas perfect usually gives anteriority relative to an orientation time supplied elsewhere.
condition: Distinguish preterite tense inflection from perfect have in direct and compound temporal relations.

correct.text: The driver departed yesterday.
The driver had departed before the inspection began.

concept: Inflectional primary versus analytic secondary tense
statement: Primary tense is inflectionally marked and contrasts past with present; perfect is a less grammaticalised analytic category marked with auxiliary have and contrasted with its absence.
condition: Compare a preterite/non-preterite verb inflection against perfect and non-perfect auxiliary structures.

correct.text: They open the office early; they opened it yesterday.

concept: Preterite also marks remoteness and backshift
statement: Unlike perfect, whose normal contribution is anteriority, the preterite has extended grammatical uses for modal remoteness and non-deictic backshift.

concept: Perfect expresses anteriority where primary past unavailable
statement: Perfect can indicate earlier situation time when preterite is already used for remoteness/backshift or when a non-finite clause cannot carry a primary preterite.

concept: Imperative temporal reference despite tenseless verb
statement: An imperative with plain-form verb normally concerns an action immediately following the utterance, despite the lack of primary tense on the verb.
condition: A plain-form imperative issues a directive to an addressee.

correct.text: Close the shutters now.

concept: Matrix time as anchor for a non-finite complement
statement: A tenseless gerund-participial complement can refer to a situation earlier than, simultaneous with, or later than the time of its catenative matrix verb.
condition: A gerund-participial clause is governed by a catenative matrix predicate.

correct.text: I recalled meeting the chairperson last spring. [earlier than recall]
I enjoyed watching the parade. [simultaneous]
I intended visiting the site the following week. [later than intend]

concept: Five classes of catenative temporal interpretation
statement: Catenative predicates can select complements whose reference time is anterior, anterior or simultaneous, simultaneous, simultaneous or posterior, or posterior to matrix time.
condition: A non-finite complement of a catenative verb is interpreted through the matrix predicate's lexical temporal selection.

correct.text: I remember telling her the date. [anterior]
She seems to know the answer. [simultaneous]

concept: Remember and forget differ by complement type
statement: Remember and forget with gerund-participials express an anterior remembered or forgotten event, whereas their infinitival constructions are a separate lexical use.
condition: A memory predicate takes a gerund-participial or to-infinitival complement.

concept: Aspectuality distinguishes anterior and simultaneous Class 2 complements
statement: With verbs such as resent and regret, a bounded-event complement is naturally anterior while a state complement can be simultaneous with the matrix.
condition: A Class 2 catenative predicate governs a perfective-event or imperfective-state complement.

The visitor may arrive tomorrow. [posterior event]

concept: Perfect auxiliaries are not selectable by all catenatives
statement: A perfect in a non-finite complement is licensed by many catenatives but not by predicates such as begin and causative make when they temporally tie matrix and complement together.
condition: A catenative takes a non-finite clause headed by perfect have, with an independently anterior subordinate event.
violation: A catenative that excludes an independently anterior perfect complement is incorrectly followed by perfect have in a single bound catenative construction.
